Lotfi Piano: Academy

I redesigned the Academy on Lotfi Piano's Iran site, a platform where piano specialists register and piano buyers can find the specialist they need and get in touch, replacing a page that did not make its purpose clear.

RoleUX/UI Designer + QA (Freelance, Part-time)
TimelineJan 2026 – Present
ScopeIran site Academy, plus audits of the Iran and Dubai sites
ToolsFigma, Microsoft Clarity, Trello

Part 1 · The Academy

Why the Academy exists

Every student who learns from a piano teacher eventually needs to buy a piano, so teachers recommend Lotfi Piano to their students. The Academy gives teachers and other piano specialists a place to register their profiles, and gives people who plan to buy a piano a place to find a specialist and contact them directly. It covers six roles: schools, teachers, tuning technicians, digital piano repairers, restorers, and piano movers.

The problem

The old page never made the Academy's purpose clear. Each role had its own section, so visitors had to scroll the whole page to learn who it served. Every role filled in the same information, the membership and review process was unclear, specialists were hard to find, and there was nowhere to get answers. The client was unhappy with it and wanted the Academy menu rebuilt so they could advertise it on social media.

Click an image to enlarge.

What I decided

  • State the Academy's purpose in the header.
  • Two primary actions: join the Academy (for specialists) and search for a specialist (for buyers).
  • Split registration into six steps. The role someone picks decides which steps differ, because some information is shared and some is not (a school and a teacher need different details).
  • Add a request-tracking button under the hero, so applicants can see which stage their application is in. Lotfi Piano reviews each profile before it is published.
  • Organize the page by role, with the review process and FAQ one click away.

Request tracking. The old Academy had no way to track a request, so I added a request-tracking page. After submitting, a request has one of three statuses: under review, needs corrections, or approved. When it needs corrections, the page lists each step that needs completing or fixing, with the reviewer's comment and an orange “needs editing” tag. An “Edit information” button takes the applicant back into the six registration steps to make the changes.

The six-step registration

Registration collects information in six steps. Some steps are the same for every role; others change with the role chosen in step one.

1 Same for all roles

Membership type

Choose one of six roles: music school, piano teacher, tuning technician, digital piano repairer, piano restorer, or piano mover. The role decides what some later steps ask for.

2 Different for schools

Basic information

  • Personal information, profile information, and work location.
  • Schools: school identity, school introduction, and work location.
3 Varies by role

Specialist information

  • Teacher: teaching field, class information, about the teacher.
  • School: educational services, about the school.
  • Tuning technician: work experience, service area, introduction to their specialty.
  • Digital piano repairer, restorer, piano mover: service location, how the service is provided, introduction to their specialty.
4 Varies by role

Documents and portfolio

  • Teacher: certificates and degrees, visual portfolio.
  • School: official license, certificates.
  • Other roles: work samples and images.
5 Same for all roles

Contact methods

Enter any contact methods and choose which ones appear on the public profile.

6 Same for all roles

Review and submit

Review the information, confirm it is accurate, and submit it to Lotfi Piano for review.

After step six, Lotfi Piano reviews the information, and the profile of the person or school is then published in the Academy.

Request status: Under reviewNeeds correctionsApproved

How I worked

Before designing, I researched the registration flow and wrote a document listing what each role must provide at each step. I checked it with the client, then gave it to the developer so the information architecture could be built from it. I designed in Figma while the client followed the file, then walked the developers through the flows, with the business rules written beside each frame. After implementation I tested the build, sent fixes to the developer, and retested.

Outcome

The client was happy with the result. The Academy has not been promoted on social media or city banners yet, so there are no usage results; feedback so far is the client's.

Part 2 · Beyond the Academy

Other work on this project

The Academy was one part of my work on Lotfi Piano. This is the rest of it, in short.

Lotfi Piano runs two websites on separate domains for two audiences: lotfipiano.com for Iran and lotfipiano.ae for Dubai. I reviewed the Iran and Dubai sites and changed the flows, the information architecture, and other parts. In some parts of the site, how text was shown for SEO mattered more for attracting customers, so, in coordination with the team, I gave SEO higher priority for the business.

Auditing both sites separately

The client was not happy with the site and asked me to review it. I audited the Iran and Dubai sites separately, piece by piece (flows, information structure, presentation, UI, and anything else I noticed), documented the changes needed with suggestions for improving each part, and handed this to the client and the project manager.

I reviewed them separately because parts of the content and menus differed between the two markets. In Dubai, acoustic pianos matter most and digital pianos are a lower priority. In Iran, digital pianos need to appear clearly in the categories, because given local budgets they are the more affordable option for buyers.

Then, in agreement with the client, I moved to wireframes and to fixing the flows and information structure. The menu, the slider and hero, images, content, fonts, and CTAs all changed. On the Dubai site I reworked the images, copy, and buttons, and the client said the result was excellent.

Compare Pianos

The compare flow was broken: adding a second piano sent users back to the first piano's page, so I proposed a side panel to choose the second one. On mobile the page also scrolled sideways, did not make clear which two products were compared, and listed specs without groups. Even after implementation the layout was not right, so I designed a mobile layout to show the developers the structure to build. I recommended limiting comparison to two products; the developers built it for up to four.

Product detail page

In the old product page, the specs sat in one ungrouped list beside the product, and the price looked like a button: selecting it added the product to the cart, but it was unclear whether it was meant to be a highlighted price or an action. In my new design the price and the Add to Cart button are separate, and specs, details, and customer reviews sit in three tabs, so people switch between them to reach all the information.

Iran site and payment

On the Iran site, instead of reworking the information architecture, I improved the experience inside the existing structure and SEO requirements. Payment flows differ per market, so each site got its own.

Testing and QA

After implementation I tested the pages myself, reported issues to developers, and retested after fixes. I also reviewed user behavior with Microsoft Clarity.

Cando

I was the UX/UI designer on Cando, a building charge management app for managers, owners, tenants, and board members, across modules such as accounting, elections, and reservations.

RoleUX/UI Designer
TimelineAbout Oct 2021 – May 2025
ScopeBuilding charge management app, several modules
ToolsAdobe XD, Figma

What Cando is

Cando is a building charge management app, built at Taav System to simplify charges for complexes and apartments and to manage costs and income across kinds of use (residential, commercial, office, and more). It was the first project I took on after joining the company, and I was its UX/UI designer.

See Cando on the Taav System site →

Who it is for, and what it covers

Who it is for: complex managers, owners, and tenants, people who always worry about calculating and paying the charge, and about avoiding disputes over it.

Roles: complex (apartment) manager, unit owner, unit tenant, board members with different roles, and block representatives.

Modules: complexes, accounting (recording and calculating expenses), elections, reservations, and reports.

What I designed. I designed all the modules except reports. For reports, I designed the unit-level financial reports for managers and residents; the broader reports were handled by the developers and a new team member. Later, a junior designer joined to help me, and I handed over the redesign of the units list, the app login, and other parts we agreed needed improvement.

The problem

In most buildings, residents pay a monthly charge into the building manager's account, but they do not know what kinds of costs it covers or how much is spent on each. The main challenge was making financial information clear for the manager and the residents (owners and tenants).

How I worked

  • My role covered research, documentation, benchmarking, sketching, wireframes, a prototype, and UI.
  • I worked directly with the PO on the requirements. With the project manager, we also held regular meetings with the development team to review backlogs and prepare demos of the software.
  • I got a list of requirements from the product owner (PO), who explained what the business needed.
  • I did R&D: what a building charge is, how it is calculated and by which criteria, and how local and international apps handle it.
  • I wrote documents for the research parts, so the rest of the team could use them.
  • I analyzed each requirement and, when there was time, sketched by hand and agreed on the sketch with the PO.
  • I designed in Adobe XD (early on) and then Figma, with flows for each role and scenario the business needed, and checked the result with the PO again until I had approval.
  • I presented the flows to the team in a meeting, and the team then analyzed and implemented them.
  • After implementation, we reviewed the built version together in a demo with the whole team and the PO, covering the business rules and the implemented process.

Key decisions

Charge transparency. The manager can record costs and income in each category. When the monthly charge is calculated, residents receive the amount to pay and can also see the breakdown of costs and income, so it is clear what the charge covers.

Roles and access. The most important information for each building was its costs and income, entered by the manager. Residents (owners and tenants) can see it but cannot edit it. The monthly charge is also set by the manager, and residents cannot edit it.

Registering a complex. Because the app had to support everything from a small apartment building to a large complex, entering the complex, its blocks, and its units was redesigned several times; the challenges of large complexes were the main target. In the end, I split the registration into parts and divided the initial information between the manager role and the unit owner role.

Outcome and learnings

This project gave me deeper experience in designing varied user flows for different user roles. Cando was tried in one complex and is part of Taav System's software sales system on its site; it has not been published on public app marketplaces, so there are no usage results.

GreenDib

I designed the Groups section of GreenDib's CO₂ tracking app, a project I joined while it was in progress, and the landing pages for its ESG and AWG products.

RoleUX/UI Designer (Freelance)
TimelineJan 2026 – Present
ScopeGroups in the CO₂ app, and the ESG and AWG landing pages
ToolsFigma

Part 1 · The app

What GreenDib is

GreenDib builds digital products and solutions around sustainability, including a CO₂ tracking app and landing pages for its products.

How I joined

I joined a project that was already in progress, and several designers had worked with the team before me. I work with GreenDib as a freelance UX/UI designer.

Groups in the CO₂ app

The app has a Groups menu for companies that want to use it for their organization. They can create, edit, delete, and view each group, and after creating a group they choose its people. Based on each person's use, the group's total and daily CO₂ is shown.

Groups exist so that each organization can use the app in a way that fits it better, in line with the app's goal.

How I worked on Groups. I received an initial wireframe of the desktop version, analyzed it, and asked the developer and the client about the points that were unclear, so I could design the flow with a better view. Then I designed the flow and the UI. After that, I reviewed the flow with the developer who was already on the team, we went through the challenges, and I handed it over to them.

Login and sign-up. I also worked on changes to the login and sign-up flow.

Outcome and learnings

The client's feedback was good, and the app design is likely to be built in the near future.

Part 2 · The landing pages

Two landing pages

Alongside the app, I worked on the landing pages. This is that part.

I designed the landing pages for two of the products, ESG and AWG (Atmospheric Water Generation). The ESG page is a new version that replaces an earlier landing page that was very general. AWG had no landing page before, so that page is new. Both introduce GreenDib and what it does, and let people interested in the app fill in a form, so GreenDib can stay in touch with them about updates and products.

The ESG landing page, my Figma design. Click the image to see the full page.

ESG

The ESG page is about helping organizations make sustainability information clearer and more actionable, and organize complex data, so they can see where they stand (visibility), keep track of it over time (monitoring), and prepare reports (reporting).

Page sections

HeroChallengeSolutionHow It WorksDesigned for OrganisationsOur ApproachFAQRegister Your InterestContact

Simplifying ESG information. Instead of showing a lot of information on one page, I split the content into sections such as Challenge, Solution, How It Works, Use Cases, and Key Benefits, so a visitor understands the main idea first and then goes into detail. The goal was to make the information easier to scan for business and investor audiences.

AWG

The AWG page is about producing water from ambient air, for places where usual water infrastructure is limited.
